cards.title: CD371-targeted CAR T cells secreting interleukin-18 exhibit robust expansion and clear refractory acute myeloid leukemia.
cards.summary: A phase 1 pilot trial treated 5 patients with relapsed/refractory AML using CD371-targeted CAR T cells carrying a mutated CD28 costimulatory domain and constitutive IL-18 secretion, reporting CAR T expansion and AML clearance in 3 heavily pretreated post-transplant patients, with dose-limiting toxicity at the higher of two dose levels.
cards.modality: Autologous-style armored CAR T cell therapy (CD371-directed, IL-18 secreting)

facts.value: CD371 CAR with mutated CD28 costimulatory domain plus constitutive IL-18 secretion
facts.quote: CAR T cells targeting CD371 with a mutated CD28 costimulatory domain to limit T-cell exhaustion, and constitutive interleukin-18 (IL-18) secretion to enhance immune function (CD371/SAVVY/IL-18 CAR)

facts.value: Relapsed/refractory acute myeloid leukemia
facts.quote: 5 patients with relapsed/refractory AML

facts.value: Human phase 1 trial (NCT06017258)
facts.quote: We initiated a phase 1 trial (NCT06017258)

facts.value: 5 patients
facts.quote: administered CD371/SAVVY/IL-18 CAR T cells in 5 patients

facts.value: Single infusion
facts.quote: observed expansion following a single infusion

facts.value: 3 x 10^4 or 3 x 10^5 CAR T cells per kg
facts.quote: a single infusion of 3 × 104 or 3 × 105 CAR T cells per kg

facts.value: 3 patients refractory to 5 or more prior lines and post-allogeneic transplant cleared AML, with no GVHD
facts.quote: 3 patients refractory to ≥5 lines of therapy and postallogeneic transplant exhibited AML clearance and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease

facts.value: DLT in both patients at 3 x 10^5 per kg: prolonged cytopenias with marrow hypoplasia and severe CRS, prompting dose reduction
facts.quote: Dose-limiting toxicity in the 2 patients treated with 3 × 105 CAR T cells per kg dose (prolonged cytopenias with marrow hypoplasia; severe cytokine release syndrome) led to dose reduction

facts.value: Product manufactured successfully for the treated patients
facts.quote: successfully manufactured and administered CD371/SAVVY/IL-18 CAR T cells

facts.value: Circulating CAR T cells characterized 2 weeks after infusion
facts.quote: circulating CAR T cells in responders included predominantly cytotoxic CD8+ effector T cells 2 weeks after infusion

red_flags.flag: Dose-limiting toxicity at the higher dose level
red_flags.why: Both patients at 3 x 10^5 per kg had DLT including severe CRS and marrow hypoplasia, which forced a 10-fold dose reduction and narrows the therapeutic window.
red_flags.quote: Dose-limiting toxicity in the 2 patients treated with 3 × 105 CAR T cells per kg dose (prolonged cytopenias with marrow hypoplasia; severe cytokine release syndrome)

red_flags.why: Five treated patients across two dose levels, with 3 responders, cannot support efficacy claims and there is no comparator arm.
red_flags.quote: administered CD371/SAVVY/IL-18 CAR T cells in 5 patients with relapsed/refractory AML

red_flags.flag: No durability or follow-up duration reported
red_flags.why: The abstract gives cell phenotype at 2 weeks but does not state how long AML clearance lasted, relapse rate, or survival.

red_flags.flag: Prolonged cytopenias suggest on-target hematopoietic toxicity
red_flags.why: CD371 is expressed on normal myeloid progenitors, and marrow hypoplasia raises the question of whether a transplant rescue is required; the abstract does not address count recovery.
red_flags.quote: prolonged cytopenias with marrow hypoplasia

red_flags.flag: Cell source and manufacturing detail not stated
red_flags.why: Patients were post-allogeneic transplant, but the abstract does not say whether the product was autologous, donor-derived, vector type, transduction efficiency, or yield.

red_flags.flag: No immunogenicity or IL-18 systemic exposure data
red_flags.why: Constitutive cytokine secretion carries systemic toxicity risk and anti-CAR immune response risk; neither is reported.

open_questions: How long did the AML clearances last, and what were MRD status, relapse and survival outcomes at the latest follow-up?
Did patients with prolonged cytopenias and marrow hypoplasia recover counts, or did they require stem cell boost or transplant?
What were serum IL-18 and cytokine levels over time, and how do they relate to CRS severity and CAR T persistence?
cards.commercial_note: Activity in patients refractory to five or more prior lines after allogeneic transplant would address a real unmet need in AML, but dose-limiting marrow toxicity and severe CRS at the higher dose, plus only 5 patients treated, leave the therapeutic window and developability unproven.

cards.title: International consensus guidelines for the conduct and reporting of CAR T-cell clinical trials in AML.
cards.summary: An international workshop of AML CAR T-cell investigators produced consensus guidelines on clinical trial design and reporting, prompted by high toxicity, low response rates and inconsistent reporting across early trials.
cards.modality: CAR-T

facts.value: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
facts.quote: patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

facts.value: Early clinical experience with AML CAR T-cell therapy shows high rates of toxicities
facts.quote: beset by high rates of toxicities

facts.value: Early clinical experience shows low rates of response
facts.quote: low rates of response

red_flags.flag: Field-level poor efficacy and high toxicity
red_flags.why: The authors state that AML CAR T-cell therapy to date has shown high toxicity and low response, which signals a difficult indication for any program.
red_flags.quote: beset by high rates of toxicities and low rates of response

red_flags.why: Variability in trial design, toxicity definitions and reporting makes cross-trial comparisons and benchmarking of any single asset unreliable.
red_flags.quote: hinders the field's ability to compare study outcomes

red_flags.why: This is a consensus white paper. The abstract does not state any patient numbers, targets, doses or outcome figures.
The abstract does not state what the consensus criteria actually are, so their impact on trial design cannot be judged from it.

open_questions: Which specific design, toxicity-definition and correlative-data standards were agreed, and how do they differ from current lymphoma or ALL CAR T conventions?
Which antigen targets and on-target off-tumor toxicities (for example myeloablation) drove the unique clinical challenges described?
Have regulators or sponsors committed to adopting these reporting criteria in ongoing AML CAR T trials?
cards.commercial_note: The abstract describes AML CAR T-cell therapy as having high toxicity and low response so far, which suggests commercial value in this indication remains unproven, though standardized reporting could make it easier to compare and judge competing programs.

cards.title: TSCM-predominant allogeneic anti-BCMA CAR-T therapy for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma: preclinical characterization and interim results from a phase 1 trial.
cards.summary: Poseida's P-BCMA-ALLO1, an allogeneic TSCM-predominant anti-BCMA CAR-T, was characterized in mouse xenografts and in an interim phase 1 readout where 9 of 11 patients given enhanced lymphodepletion responded, with CRS limited to grade 2 or lower across all 33 patients.
cards.modality: Allogeneic BCMA CAR-T cell therapy

facts.value: BCMA-directed CAR
facts.quote: P-BCMA-ALLO1, a TSCM-predominant allogeneic CAR-T therapy targeting BCMA

facts.value: Heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma
facts.quote: in heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma

facts.value: Allogeneic, TSCM-predominant product
facts.quote: a TSCM-predominant allogeneic CAR-T therapy

facts.value: Mouse xenograft models preclinically; human phase 1
facts.quote: in vivo potency in mouse xenograft models

facts.value: 33 evaluable patients total, 11 in the enhanced lymphodepletion group
facts.quote: among the 11 of 33 evaluable patients who received enhanced lymphodepletion

facts.value: 82% (9/11) response rate, 63.6% (7/11) VGPR or better in the enhanced lymphodepletion group
facts.quote: 82% (9/11) responded, with 63.6% (7/11) achieving very good partial response (VGPR) or better

facts.value: CRS in 21.2% (7/33), all grade 2 or lower
facts.quote: CRS was reported in 21.2% (7/33) across all cohorts, all grade ≤2.

facts.value: Peak CAR-T expansion at a median of 10 days post-infusion, with persistence seen in bone marrow
facts.quote: The median time to peak CAR-T cell expansion (Tmax) was 10 days post-infusion.

facts.value: 100% intent-to-treat infusion rate, treatment started a median of 1 day after enrollment, no bridging therapy
facts.quote: All patients started therapy a median of 1 day after enrollment, with every patient receiving P-BCMA-ALLO1 infusion, and resulting in a 100% intent-to-treat (ITT) rate with no use of bridging therapy.

red_flags.flag: Efficacy reported only in a selected subgroup
red_flags.why: Response rates come from 11 of 33 patients who got enhanced lymphodepletion; the abstract does not give response rates for the other 22 patients, which makes the headline figure look selected.
red_flags.quote: among the 11 of 33 evaluable patients who received enhanced lymphodepletion, 82% (9/11) responded

red_flags.why: The abstract gives expansion Tmax of 10 days but no duration of response, progression-free survival, or follow-up time.
A phase 1 dose escalation would normally report cell doses per cohort; the abstract does not state any dose.

red_flags.flag: No GvHD, allorejection or immunogenicity data
red_flags.why: For an allogeneic product the key risks are graft versus host disease and host rejection of the allogeneic cells; the abstract does not state either.
Persistence in bone marrow is asserted without timepoints or quantitative measures.
red_flags.quote: with trafficking and persistence observed in bone marrow

red_flags.why: ICANS and infection rates after enhanced lymphodepletion are standard safety reporting and are not stated.
No benchmark against autologous BCMA CAR-T or other allogeneic products is reported, so the claimed advantage of TSCM is not tested clinically.
red_flags.quote: a TSCM cellular phenotype may offer significant advantages in efficacy, safety, and cellular persistence

red_flags.flag: No manufacturing yield or batch data
red_flags.why: Allogeneic value depends on doses per donor batch and release success; the abstract reports only turnaround time to infusion.

open_questions: What were the response rates, dose levels and lymphodepletion regimens in the 22 patients outside the enhanced lymphodepletion cohort?
What is the median duration of response and follow-up, and how long do CAR-T cells persist after the day 10 expansion peak?
What rates of GvHD, ICANS, infection and host-mediated rejection were seen, and how many doses are produced per donor apheresis?
cards.commercial_note: An off-the-shelf BCMA CAR-T that reached 100% intent-to-treat with a median of 1 day from enrollment to start and no bridging therapy would address the main logistical weakness of autologous products, but the efficacy claim rests on 11 patients in a selected subgroup with no durability data.

cards.title: Adeno-associated vector corneal gene therapy reverses corneal clouding in a feline model of mucopolysaccharidosis VI.
cards.summary: Intrastromal AAV8 carrying an optimized human ARSB cassette at 1e9 vector genomes reversed pre-existing corneal clouding within 2-3 weeks in a naturally occurring feline model of MPS VI, with improved stromal morphology and detectable human ARSB in the stroma.
cards.modality: AAV gene therapy (AAV8, corneal intrastromal gene addition)

facts.value: AAV serotype 8 capsid, single-stranded genome
facts.quote: The AAV serotype 8 capsid was packaged with a single-strand optimized human ARSB expression cassette (optARSB)

facts.value: codon-optimized human ARSB expression cassette
facts.quote: a single-strand optimized human ARSB expression cassette (optARSB)

facts.value: Mucopolysaccharidosis VI corneal clouding
facts.quote: Ocular manifestations of MPS VI include progressive corneal clouding, leading to vision loss.

facts.value: cornea, stroma
facts.quote: administered to MPS VI feline corneas at a dose of 1e9 vector genomes via intrastromal injection

facts.value: naturally occurring feline MPS VI model
facts.quote: evaluated in a naturally occurring MPS VI feline model

facts.value: intrastromal injection, including sequential contralateral dosing at 7 weeks
facts.quote: Sequential dosing of the contralateral cornea 7 weeks after the first dose also cleared the storage disease with similar kinetics

facts.value: 1e9 vector genomes per cornea
facts.quote: at a dose of 1e9 vector genomes via intrastromal injection

facts.value: complete reversal of pre-existing clouding in 2-3 weeks; improved stromal organization; ARSB present throughout stroma; less smooth muscle actin staining
facts.quote: resulting in a complete reversal of pre-existing corneal clouding within 2-3 weeks, which was maintained throughout the study

facts.value: maintained for the duration of the study (length not given)
facts.quote: which was maintained throughout the study

facts.value: all injections reported well tolerated
facts.quote: All AAV8-optARSB injections were well tolerated

facts.value: untreated MPS VI animals used as comparison for corneal morphology
facts.quote: revealed disorganization in the posterior corneal stroma in untreated animals

red_flags.why: The abstract never states how many cats or eyes were treated, so effect robustness cannot be judged.
Durability is claimed as maintained "throughout the study" without saying how long that was.
red_flags.quote: which was maintained throughout the study

red_flags.why: The abstract reports tolerability but no anti-AAV or anti-human ARSB antibody or T cell data, which matters given a xenogeneic human transgene in cats and sequential second-eye dosing.

red_flags.flag: No vector biodistribution or shedding data
red_flags.why: Intrastromal AAV can leak to anterior chamber and systemically; the abstract gives no quantification.

red_flags.flag: No quantitative enzyme activity or GAG storage measures reported
red_flags.why: Efficacy rests on imaging and staining; no ARSB activity units or glycosaminoglycan reduction numbers are stated.
red_flags.quote: Human arylsulfatase B was observed throughout the corneal stroma with decreased smooth muscle actin staining

red_flags.flag: No manufacturing, titer or purity information
red_flags.why: Nothing on vector production, yield, or release testing is provided.
MPS VI is systemic, so a local corneal treatment leaves other organ manifestations untreated and the abstract does not address this.
red_flags.quote: Mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS VI) is a rare, autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease

red_flags.flag: Single dose level, no dose ranging
red_flags.why: Only 1e9 vg was tested, justified by prior MPS I work rather than by a dose response in this model.
red_flags.quote: as this strategy relied on the same AAV capsid, vector dose, genetic cassette context, injection type, and volume deemed safe and effective for the treatment of MPS I

open_questions: How many animals and eyes were treated, and for how many months was clarity followed after dosing?
What anti-AAV8 and anti-human ARSB immune responses were measured, especially before the second-eye dose at 7 weeks?
What were quantitative corneal ARSB activity and GAG storage levels relative to wild type, and was there any vector spread beyond the cornea?
cards.commercial_note: A low dose, locally delivered vector that reverses existing corneal clouding could offer an alternative to corneal transplant in a rare disease and, if the shared capsid, dose and delivery with the MPS I program hold, could support a platform across corneal lysosomal storage indications, though the market is small and systemic disease still needs separate treatment.

cards.title: Characterizing and controlling CRISPR repair outcomes in nondividing human cells.
cards.summary: Using iPSCs and iPSC-derived neurons, the authors compared Cas9-induced DNA repair in postmitotic versus dividing human cells and showed that chemical or genetic perturbation of non-canonical repair factors can shift editing outcomes in neurons, cardiomyocytes and primary T cells.
cards.modality: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (repair outcome control)

facts.value: Cas9-induced DNA double strand breaks; delivery method not stated
facts.quote: examine how postmitotic human neurons repair Cas9-induced DNA damage

facts.value: Human iPSCs and iPSC-derived neurons, plus cardiomyocytes and primary T cells
facts.quote: using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and iPSC-derived neurons

facts.value: Nondividing human neurons, cardiomyocytes, primary T cells
facts.quote: nondividing human neurons, cardiomyocytes, and primary T cells

facts.value: Perturbations directed repair toward desired editing outcomes in nondividing cells
facts.quote: Manipulating this response with chemical or genetic perturbations allows us to direct DNA repair toward desired editing outcomes

facts.value: Genetically identical dividing cells
facts.quote: CRISPR editing outcomes differ dramatically in neurons compared to genetically identical dividing cells

red_flags.flag: All work appears to be in vitro cell culture
red_flags.why: No animal or in vivo demonstration is described, so translational relevance to tissues like brain or heart is untested.

red_flags.flag: No editing efficiency or precision numbers
red_flags.why: The abstract gives no percentages for indel, HDR or desired outcome rates, so the size of the effect cannot be judged.

red_flags.flag: No target gene or indication named
red_flags.why: The work is mechanistic; no disease target or therapeutic hypothesis is stated.

red_flags.flag: No off-target, p53 response or toxicity data
red_flags.why: Manipulating DNA repair pathways chemically or genetically raises genome stability and safety concerns that the abstract does not address.
red_flags.quote: Manipulating this response with chemical or genetic perturbations

red_flags.flag: No delivery, dose or manufacturing detail
red_flags.why: Nothing is said about how Cas9 is delivered or at what dose, which determines whether the approach is deliverable in vivo.
Repair is said to take longer in neurons but no long term persistence or stability of edits is reported.
red_flags.quote: neurons take longer to fully resolve this damage

red_flags.flag: Sample sizes and replicates not stated
red_flags.why: Claims of dramatic differences cannot be weighed without n.

open_questions: What absolute editing and precise repair rates were achieved in neurons before and after perturbation, and with what variance across donors?
Which specific chemical and genetic perturbations were used, and do they increase off-target edits, large deletions or chromosomal instability?
Does the approach work in vivo with a realistic delivery vehicle, and for how long do edited cells persist?
cards.commercial_note: If repair modulation reliably raises precise editing in postmitotic neurons and cardiomyocytes, it could be licensed as an adjunct to in vivo editing programs in CNS and cardiac disease, but the abstract reports no efficiency numbers, delivery route or safety data to support that yet.

cards.title: Glutarimide-derived ionizable lipid enables mRNA lipid nanoparticle vaccines with enhanced safety and immunogenicity.
cards.summary: The authors synthesized a glutarimide-derived ionizable lipid (MOP-1), formulated it into mRNA LNPs, and reported good tolerability plus humoral and CD8+ T-cell responses with 90% survival after lethal influenza challenge in animals.
cards.modality: LNP mRNA vaccine with novel ionizable lipid

facts.value: Lipid nanoparticle built on new ionizable lipid MOP-1
facts.quote: an innovative glutarimide-derived ionizable lipid, MOP-1, that enables an LNP with high delivery efficiency and a favorable safety profile

facts.value: Influenza mRNA vaccine antigen
facts.quote: When evaluated as an influenza mRNA vaccine platform

facts.value: Influenza prophylaxis
facts.quote: excellent protection against a lethal viral challenge

facts.value: 90 % survival and near-complete viral clearance after lethal challenge
facts.quote: with a 90 % survival rate and near-complete viral clearance

facts.value: High neutralizing antibody and CD8+ T-cell responses
facts.quote: induced robust humoral and cellular immune responses, including high neutralizing antibody production and CD8+ T-cell activation

facts.value: No cytotoxicity in vitro, no organ damage in vivo at high doses, controlled cytokine profile
facts.quote: negligible in vitro cytotoxicity and no evidence of organ damage in vivo even at high doses

facts.value: High colloidal stability and acid dissociation suited to endosomal escape
facts.quote: including high colloidal stability and favorable acid dissociation characteristics for efficient endosomal escape

red_flags.why: The abstract says in vivo and lethal challenge but never names the animal model, so translatability and challenge strain cannot be judged.
Claims of safety at high doses and of potency are unverifiable without mg/kg or microgram dose and injection route.
red_flags.quote: no evidence of organ damage in vivo even at high doses

red_flags.why: A 90% survival figure implies about 10 animals per group but sample size is not stated, so the statistical weight is unknown.
Superiority claims are made against current LNP platforms without naming MC3, ALC-0315 or SM-102 data in the abstract.
red_flags.quote: avoids excessive inflammatory responses associated with current LNP platforms

red_flags.why: Antibody titer persistence and duration of protection after challenge are not reported.
Colloidal stability is asserted without storage temperature, time or lipid degradation data.
red_flags.quote: including high colloidal stability

red_flags.why: Language such as transformative and exceptional overstates preclinical single-antigen data.
red_flags.quote: MOP-1-LNPs could become a transformative mRNA delivery system

red_flags.why: Platform breadth is claimed from one influenza vaccine experiment.
red_flags.quote: may enable broader applications in prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine development

open_questions: What species, strain, dose, route and group size were used for the lethal challenge, and what was the control arm survival?
How does MOP-1 compare head-to-head with MC3, SM-102 or ALC-0315 on potency, reactogenicity and cytokine release at matched doses?
What are the biodegradability, biodistribution and long-term antibody persistence data for MOP-1 LNPs, and is the lipid freely synthesizable at scale?
cards.commercial_note: A new ionizable lipid that claims reduced reactogenicity could carve out freedom to operate around existing lipid patents and support higher dosing, but the abstract gives no comparator data, dose or species to support that claim.

facts.quote: Clinical-scale manufacturing from a patient

red_flags.quote: The resulting gcTregs demonstrated robust suppressive activity in vitro.

open_questions: What were the HDR correction rates, final cell yields, and off-target/translocation profiles in the clinical-scale run?
Does mono-allelic correction restore IL2RA surface levels and IL-2 signaling to healthy donor levels, and is the second allele targetable?
Is there any in vivo data on gcTreg persistence, stability of FOXP3 phenotype, and disease control before a first-in-human trial?
cards.commercial_note: The target population is extremely small, since the work stems from a single family with a rare bi-allelic defect, so value rests on the claim that the GMP-compatible process is a framework for other inborn errors of immunity rather than on IL2RA deficiency itself.

Did response or persistence differ between autologous and donor-derived products, and what is the recommended phase 2 dose?
cards.commercial_note: r/r AML after alloHCT has few options and the safety profile here looked manageable, but a modest CR rate with limited persistence suggests this construct would need redesign before it has commercial value.

cards.commercial_note: Strong early response but a 6.1 month median relapse-free survival and frequent IEC-HS suggest this construct alone is weak as a product, and the authors themselves frame it as a foundation for newer CD22 and dual-targeting approaches.

cards.title: Virus-like particles enable targeted gene engineering and pooled CRISPR screening in primary human myeloid cells.

cards.title: Systemic Inflammation and CAR-T Specific Toxicities as Major Drivers of Nonrelapse Mortality: Analysis from the Italian Prospective Observational CART-SIE Study.

cards.title: BACH2 regulates T cell lineage state to enhance CAR T cell function.
cards.summary: The authors show that 41BB costimulation induces the transcription factor BACH2, and that drug-tunable BACH2 overexpression via a degradation domain prevents CAR T cell exhaustion while preserving effector function and improving long-term efficacy against liquid and solid tumor models, with BACH2 activity also associated with clinical outcomes in leukemia patients.

open_questions: Which antigen and tumor models were used, and what CAR T doses and follow-up durations supported the long-term efficacy claim?

cards.commercial_note: A tunable switch that separates exhaustion resistance from effector function could be licensed as an add-on module across existing CAR programs, including solid tumors, but the abstract gives no antigen, in vivo dosing, safety, or manufacturing detail to judge readiness.

facts.quote: Patients (n = 26) were randomly allocated to receive once-weekly intravenous infusions of Descartes-08 (n = 15) or placebo (n = 11)

facts.value: Intravenous infusion
facts.quote: once-weekly intravenous infusions

facts.value: Six once-weekly infusions over 6 weeks; cell dose per infusion not given
facts.quote: a single course of six once-weekly infusions

facts.value: Placebo
facts.quote: placebo (n = 11)

facts.value: Month 3 MGC improvement of 5 points or more: 66.7% (n = 10/15) vs 27.3% (n = 3/11), P = 0.0472
AChR antibody-positive subgroup: 63.6% (n = 7/11) vs 12.5% (n = 1/8), P = 0.0258
Treated-arm mean changes at month 4: MGC -7.1, MG-ADL -5.5, QMG -4.8
facts.quote: at month 4 were -7.1, -5.5 and -4.8, respectively

facts.value: 33.0% reached minimum symptom expression by month 6; 55.60% among biologic-naive patients
facts.quote: 33.0% of patients achieved minimum symptom expression (MSE)

facts.value: 83.0% of treated patients had a sustained, clinically meaningful response at month 12; MSE maintained through month 12 without additional treatment in biologic-naive patients
facts.quote: 83.0% of patients achieving a sustained and clinically meaningful response at month 12

red_flags.flag: Small trial with borderline primary endpoint significance
red_flags.why: With 15 vs 11 patients, the primary result sits just under 0.05 and a single responder shift could change the conclusion.

red_flags.flag: Safety denominators do not match randomized arms
red_flags.why: Safety counts use 20 and 16 patients while efficacy uses 15 and 11; the abstract does not explain the difference (for example crossover or a separate safety set).

red_flags.flag: Durability and MSE figures lack denominators and placebo comparison
red_flags.why: 83.0%, 33.0% and 55.60% are given without counts, do not map cleanly onto 15 patients, and month 12 results are reported only for the treated arm.
red_flags.quote: 83.0% of patients achieving a sustained and clinically meaningful response at month 12

red_flags.why: The AChR-positive subgroup has 11 vs 8 patients and the biologic-naive subgroup size is unstated, so these results are fragile.
The abstract does not state the number of CAR T cells per infusion or per course.
The abstract does not state effects on autoantibody titers, plasma cell depletion, or CAR T persistence, so the link between BCMA targeting and clinical benefit is not shown.
The abstract does not state manufacturing success rate, yield, turnaround time, or cost for this autologous product.

red_flags.flag: Safety summary is qualitative beyond infusion reactions
red_flags.why: The abstract does not state serious adverse events, infections, cytopenias, or hypogammaglobulinemia rates.
red_flags.quote: Descartes-08 was generally safe and well tolerated.

open_questions: Why do safety denominators (20 and 16) differ from the randomized arms (15 and 11), and was there crossover from placebo?
What were the per-infusion cell doses, manufacturing success rate and vein-to-vein time?
How did AChR autoantibody titers and plasma cell markers change, and what are the placebo-arm results at month 12?
cards.commercial_note: A placebo-controlled signal from a fixed six-infusion course with responses reported out to 12 months could position this as a time-limited option in gMG, but the 26-patient size, borderline P value and absent manufacturing data mean a larger confirmatory trial is needed before the commercial case is clear.

cards.title: Engineering CLL-1 CAR-NK cells via mRNA-LNP for potent antitumor activity and reversal of HLA-E-mediated resistance in acute myeloid leukemia.
cards.summary: The authors used mRNA-LNP to transiently engineer primary NK cells with a CLL-1 CAR, showed antigen-specific killing of AML lines and patient blasts and survival benefit in NSG xenografts with repeated dosing, and found that tumor HLA-E upregulation via JAK2-STAT1 drives resistance that NKG2A blockade reverses.
cards.modality: mRNA-LNP engineered CAR-NK cells

facts.value: lipid nanoparticle mRNA delivery, non-integrating and transient
facts.quote: We developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)–based mRNA delivery platform for scalable generation of C-type lectin-like molecule-1 (CLL-1) CAR-NK cells.

facts.value: CLL-1 directed CAR
facts.quote: CLL-1 was the only validated CAR target upregulated

facts.value: multidrug-resistant acute myeloid leukemia
facts.quote: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains a highly lethal malignancy, with relapse primarily driven by resistance to chemotherapy or targeted therapies.

facts.value: primary NK cells
facts.quote: mRNA–LNP transfection enabled efficient generation of primary CLL-1 CAR-NK cells with preserved phenotype

facts.value: AML cell lines, patient-derived blasts, NSG mouse xenografts
facts.quote: evaluated ex vivo against AML cell lines and patient-derived blasts, with in vivo efficacy tested in xenograft NSG mouse models

facts.value: repeated infusions, number not given
facts.quote: In vivo, repeated CAR-NK infusions markedly suppressed leukemia progression and prolonged survival.

facts.value: suppressed leukemia progression and prolonged survival in vivo; NKG2A blockade further improved clearance and survival
facts.quote: NKG2A blockade restored cytotoxicity ex vivo and enhanced leukemia clearance and survival in vivo.

facts.value: spared normal hematopoietic progenitors
facts.quote: while sparing normal hematopoietic progenitors

facts.value: described as scalable mRNA-LNP generation, no yield figures
facts.quote: scalable generation of C-type lectin-like molecule-1 (CLL-1) CAR-NK cells

facts.value: JAK2 knockdown versus pharmacologic JAK2 inhibition as resistance interventions
facts.quote: JAK2 knockdown reduced HLA-E expression and sensitized AML cells to CAR-NK–mediated killing, whereas pharmacologic JAK2 inhibition also decreased HLA-E expression but concurrently impaired NK-cell activation

red_flags.flag: No quantitative data of any kind
red_flags.why: The abstract gives no transfection efficiency, CAR expression level, effector-to-target ratios, cell doses, infusion schedule, or survival numbers, so the size of the effect cannot be judged.
Mouse and patient sample numbers are not given, so the robustness of the in vivo and patient-blast results is unknown.
mRNA CAR expression lasts days, and the abstract itself ties efficacy to repeated infusions, which raises cost, logistics and durability questions.
red_flags.quote: Repeated dosing enables robust antitumor activity

red_flags.why: CAR-NK exposure itself drove HLA-E upregulation and loss of function, meaning monotherapy may fail without an added NKG2A blocking agent.
red_flags.quote: progressive HLA-E upregulation, which impaired CAR-NK function

red_flags.flag: Proposed combination partner may not work
red_flags.why: Pharmacologic JAK2 inhibition blunted NK activation, so the most tractable clinical version of the mechanism was negative.
red_flags.quote: pharmacologic JAK2 inhibition also decreased HLA-E expression but concurrently impaired NK-cell activation, thereby limiting the overall therapeutic benefit

red_flags.flag: Safety claim not supported by stated toxicology
red_flags.why: The conclusion calls the approach safe but the abstract reports only sparing of hematopoietic progenitors, with no cytokine release, LNP tolerability or on-target off-tumor data in vivo.
red_flags.quote: provide a safe and effective strategy for MDR AML

red_flags.why: No follow-up duration, persistence of CAR expression, or relapse rate after the last infusion is stated.
NSG xenografts cannot show host immune rejection of allogeneic NK cells or LNP immunogenicity.
red_flags.quote: in vivo efficacy tested in xenograft NSG mouse models

open_questions: What is the CAR transfection efficiency, peak expression level, and how many days does surface CAR persist on primary NK cells after mRNA-LNP delivery?
What cell dose, infusion number and schedule were used in the NSG model, with group sizes and median survival for each arm?
Is the NK product autologous, allogeneic donor-derived or cord blood derived, and what are batch yield and cost per dose given that repeated dosing is required?
cards.commercial_note: A non-integrating, transiently expressed CLL-1 CAR-NK made by simple mRNA-LNP transfection could be cheaper and lower risk than CAR-T for AML, but the need for repeated dosing plus an NKG2A blocking antibody to counter induced HLA-E makes it a combination product rather than a standalone therapy.

cards.title: IgM-and IgG-cleaving enzyme facilitates AAV gene transfer in AAV-seropositive macaques.
cards.summary: In AAV-seropositive, SHIV-infected rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, intravenous dosing with the engineered IgM/IgG-cleaving enzyme IceMG transiently lowered IgG, IgM and AAV9-neutralizing antibody titers and allowed a second round of AAV9 transduction and transgene expression, though AAV-neutralizing antibodies rebounded and anti-transgene antibodies arose in some animals.
cards.modality: AAV gene therapy with enzymatic antibody-cleaving pretreatment (IceMG/IdeS)

facts.value: AAV9 vector, with IceMG enzyme pretreatment
facts.quote: IceMG administration to macaques prior to AAV9 vector boosting enabled a second round of successful AAV transduction and transgene expression

facts.value: antiviral proteins intended to control HIV replication
facts.quote: long-term delivery of antiviral proteins that can control HIV replication

facts.value: HIV infection (SHIV in macaques)
facts.quote: AAV-seropositive, SHIV-infected rhesus and cynomolgus macaques

facts.value: AAV-seropositive, SHIV-infected rhesus and cynomolgus macaques
facts.quote: AAV-seropositive, SHIV-infected rhesus and cynomolgus macaques

facts.value: intravenous for the enzyme
facts.quote: Intravenous administration of IceMG to macaques

facts.value: IdeS, an IgG-only cleaving enzyme, and macaques given no IceMG before AAV boost
facts.quote: in contrast to dosing with IdeS, an IgG-specific immunoglobulin-cleaving enzyme

facts.value: Transient depletion of IgG and IgM and of AAV9 neutralizing antibodies; successful AAV re-dosing only with IceMG
facts.quote: in contrast to macaques that did not receive IceMG where AAV vector boosting failed to produce detectable transgene

facts.value: Effect transient; re-dosing months later worked as well as the first dose; transgene protein lost from circulation in some animals
facts.quote: Re-dosing macaques with IceMG or IdeS months later reduced circulating intact IgG, SHIV Env-binding IgG titers, and AAV-specific neutralizing antibody titers with similar efficacy as the initial dose.

facts.value: Enzyme dosing lowered Env-binding IgG and was linked to rises in SHIV plasma viral load; anti-drug antibodies to the transgene protein in some animals
facts.quote: which were associated with concomitant increases in SHIV plasma viral loads

red_flags.why: Stripping IgG in an infected host temporarily removed virologic control, a direct safety concern for this indication.
red_flags.quote: temporarily decreased SHIV Env-binding IgG plasma concentrations, which were associated with concomitant increases in SHIV plasma viral loads

red_flags.flag: Anti-transgene immunity and loss of expression
red_flags.why: The main value proposition, durable antiviral protein expression, failed in some animals after re-dosing.
red_flags.quote: increases in anti-drug antibodies (ADA) targeting the AAV vector transgene protein and subsequent loss of transgene protein from circulation

red_flags.flag: Neutralizing antibody rebound limits further re-dosing
red_flags.why: A third administration may be blocked, so the approach may only buy one extra dose.
red_flags.quote: AAV vector boosting also led to rebound of AAV-specific neutralizing antibody titers in all macaques

red_flags.why: The abstract states no mg/kg for IceMG or vg/kg for AAV9, so potency and vector burden cannot be judged.
Number of macaques per arm is not stated, and NHP studies are usually small, so the contrast with untreated animals may rest on very few subjects.

red_flags.flag: No immunogenicity data on the enzyme itself
red_flags.why: IceMG is an engineered bacterial-type enzyme; anti-IceMG antibodies would limit repeat use and are not reported.

red_flags.flag: No quantitative transgene expression or durability numbers
red_flags.why: Expression levels and how long they lasted after the second dose are not given.
Nothing on vector yield, purity, or enzyme production is reported.

open_questions: What IceMG dose and AAV9 vg/kg dose were used, and how many animals were in each arm?
How long did transgene expression last after the second AAV9 dose, and at what circulating protein concentration?
Did animals develop anti-IceMG antibodies, and does that block a third administration?
cards.commercial_note: Enabling a second AAV administration in seropositive primates would address a real limit on AAV redosing, but the reported rebound of neutralizing antibodies, anti-transgene ADA with loss of protein, and transient viral load increases keep the window narrow.

cards.title: Calcium Shock Enables Efficient and Programmable Particle Delivery for Genome Editing Applications.
cards.summary: The authors describe calcium shock (CaSh) and a targeted variant (CaSh-Pro), methods that raise endocytic uptake and loosen cell-cell junctions to improve delivery of plasmids, ribonucleoproteins, and AAV into cells, colonies, and organoids, including cell type selective editing in mixed populations.
cards.modality: Ex vivo delivery method for genome editing cargo (plasmid, RNP, AAV)

facts.value: Plasmid, Cas9 ribonucleoprotein, or AAV delivered with calcium shock; CaSh-Pro adds targeting agents and amphiphilic peptides
facts.quote: Calcium shock improves expression of plasmid, ribonucleoprotein, or adeno-associated viral vectors with minimal toxicity in intact organoids representing diverse lineages.

facts.value: Single cells, colonies, and organoids of diverse lineages
facts.quote: dramatically improves particle delivery into single cells, colonies, and organoids

facts.value: Intact organoids representing diverse lineages
facts.quote: in intact organoids representing diverse lineages

facts.value: Minimal toxicity reported
facts.quote: with minimal toxicity

facts.value: Compared against classical transfection and transduction
facts.quote: Classical intracellular delivery methods such as transfection and transduction are inefficient

red_flags.why: The abstract claims dramatic improvement but gives no editing percentages, fold changes, or delivery efficiency numbers.
red_flags.quote: dramatically improves particle delivery into single cells, colonies, and organoids

red_flags.why: All work described is in cultured cells and organoids, with no animal or in vivo delivery data.
red_flags.quote: in intact organoids representing diverse lineages

red_flags.why: "Minimal toxicity" is stated without viability numbers, calcium concentration, or exposure time.
red_flags.quote: with minimal toxicity

red_flags.flag: No sample size or replication stated
red_flags.why: The abstract does not state how many organoids, donors, or independent experiments were tested.
The abstract does not state how long edited or transduced cells were followed, or whether edits persist in organoid culture.
Cell type selective editing is claimed but on-target versus off-cell-type editing rates are not stated.
red_flags.quote: enables programmable delivery (CaSh-Pro) into specific cell types within heterocellular populations

red_flags.why: The abstract does not state whether genome-wide off-target editing was measured.

open_questions: What calcium concentration and exposure time are used, and what are measured viability and editing rates versus standard transfection or AAV transduction?
How selective is CaSh-Pro, quantitatively, between target and non-target cell types in a heterocellular organoid?
Does CaSh work in vivo or only in culture, and does it alter AAV serotype tropism or required vector dose?
cards.commercial_note: If the efficiency gains hold up, the value is as an ex vivo manufacturing and research tool for editing organoids and confluent cultures rather than as a therapeutic product, and the abstract gives no in vivo or clinical data to support more than that.

cards.title: Efficient targeting of human glial progenitor cells in vivo with engineered AAV vectors and glymphatic delivery.
cards.summary: The authors screened a capsid-modified AAV library in chimeric mice carrying human glial progenitor cells and identified AAV5-based capsids with tropism for human GPCs, then delivered them by intracisternal injection combined with systemic hypertonicity to boost glymphatic spread across the adult mouse brain.
cards.modality: AAV gene therapy (engineered capsid, glymphatic CNS delivery)

facts.value: Capsid-modified AAV5-based vectors selected by in vivo library screening
facts.quote: identified a set of AAV5-based vectors that preferentially infect human GPCs and/or their astrocyte and oligodendrocyte progeny in vivo

facts.value: Human glial progenitor cells and their astrocyte and oligodendrocyte progeny in brain
facts.quote: selective delivery of viral vectors to their common parent, glial progenitor cells (GPCs)

facts.value: Neurological diseases involving oligodendrocytes or astrocytes
facts.quote: Treatment of neurological diseases that involve oligodendrocytes or astrocytes

facts.value: Chimeric mice engrafted with human GPCs expressing PDGFRA-driven Cre
facts.quote: chimeric mice engrafted with PDGFRA-driven Cre recombinase-expressing human GPCs

facts.value: Intracisternal delivery paired with systemic hypertonicity to increase glymphatic influx
facts.quote: we paired intracisternal delivery with systemic hypertonicity to increase glymphatic influx

facts.value: Transgene delivery to human glia throughout the whole adult mouse brain with minimal off-target transduction
facts.quote: enables efficient transgene delivery to human glia throughout the entire adult mouse brain, with minimal off-target transduction

facts.value: Minimal systemic infection reported for selected vectors
facts.quote: with minimal systemic infection

red_flags.why: The abstract claims dose minimization but gives no vector genome dose or volume, so efficiency per genome cannot be judged.
No follow-up time or expression persistence is reported after glymphatic delivery.
Work is reporter and recombination based; no disease transgene or functional benefit in a disease model is described.
red_flags.quote: enables efficient transgene delivery to human glia throughout the entire adult mouse brain

red_flags.why: Tropism for human GPCs is shown in a single chimeric mouse model, with no large animal or primate confirmation, and intracisternal plus systemic hypertonic dosing may not translate.
red_flags.quote: In vivo screening of a library of capsid-modified, recombination-reported AAVs in chimeric mice

red_flags.why: Number of animals per group or per capsid is not stated.

red_flags.flag: No immunogenicity or neutralizing antibody data
red_flags.why: AAV5 seroprevalence and CSF route immune response are not addressed.
Capsid modifications can lower packaging yield; the abstract reports none.

red_flags.flag: Safety of systemic hypertonicity not addressed
red_flags.why: Hypertonic dosing to force glymphatic influx is a procedure with its own tolerability questions that the abstract does not discuss.
red_flags.quote: we paired intracisternal delivery with systemic hypertonicity

open_questions: What vector genome dose per animal was used, and how does transduction efficiency scale with dose?
How long does transgene expression in human GPCs and their progeny persist, and is it maintained after differentiation?
Do the selected AAV5 variants retain human GPC tropism in a large animal or non-human primate given by intracisternal route without hypertonic adjunct?
cards.commercial_note: A capsid plus delivery route that reaches glia brain-wide at low dose would be useful for oligodendrocyte and astrocyte diseases, but the package here is a reporter-stage tool with no dose, durability or therapeutic payload data.

cards.title: Cis-targeted IL-2 Mutein to Augment the Antitumor Activity of Engineered T Cells.
cards.summary: The authors built antibody-IL-2 mutein fusions that bind a marker expressed only on engineered T cells, and showed selective stimulation of CAR-T cells and engineered TILs with improved antitumor function in tumor models plus CAR-T expansion and B cell aplasia without lymphodepletion in nonhuman primates.
cards.modality: Cis-targeted IL-2 mutein antibody fusion protein paired with engineered T cells (CAR-T and TIL)

facts.value: IL-2 mutein fused to an antibody against a surface marker on engineered T cells
facts.quote: cis-targeted IL-2 fusion molecules which are comprised of an IL-2 mutein with attenuated binding to IL-2Rα and IL-2Rβ linked to an antibody that targets a cell-surface molecule expressed specifically on engineered T cells

facts.value: IL-2 mutein with reduced IL-2Ralpha and IL-2Rbeta binding
facts.quote: an IL-2 mutein with attenuated binding to IL-2Rα and IL-2Rβ

facts.value: Lymphoma and melanoma (cells from those patients used)
facts.quote: from lymphoma and melanoma patients

facts.value: T cells from healthy donors and from lymphoma and melanoma patients
facts.quote: Using T cells from healthy donors as well as from lymphoma and melanoma patients

facts.value: Multiple tumor models plus a nonhuman primate model
facts.quote: enhanced their antitumor function in multiple tumor models

facts.value: Selective stimulation of CAR-T or engineered TILs and better antitumor function; CAR-T expansion and B cell aplasia in NHP without lymphodepletion
facts.quote: cis-targeted IL-2 can mediate CART expansion and B cell aplasia in the absence of lymphodepletion in a nonhuman primate model

facts.value: Framed against lymphodepleting chemotherapy and high dose IL-2
facts.quote: Lymphodepleting chemotherapy (LDC) is associated with cytopenias and attendant complications, while high dose IL-2 causes severe infusion toxicity

red_flags.why: The abstract gives no dose, route or dosing interval for the fusion protein or the cell product, so potency and therapeutic window cannot be judged.
The premise is that high dose IL-2 is toxic, yet the abstract reports no toxicity readouts (vascular leak, cytokine release, Treg or NK expansion) for the fusion.
No follow-up duration is given for tumor control or for the NHP CAR-T expansion and B cell aplasia.
Group sizes for donors, tumor models or nonhuman primates are not stated.
A mutated human IL-2 fused to an antibody given repeatedly can draw anti-drug antibodies, especially in NHP; no anti-drug antibody data are mentioned.
The engineered-T-cell surface molecule being targeted is not identified, so specificity versus endogenous expression cannot be assessed.
red_flags.quote: an antibody that targets a cell-surface molecule expressed specifically on engineered T cells

red_flags.why: No yield, purity or stability information for the fusion protein is given.
"Multiple tumor models" without naming them makes it impossible to judge stringency or whether models are xenograft or syngeneic.
red_flags.quote: enhanced their antitumor function in multiple tumor models

open_questions: What is the targeted surface molecule, and is it expressed on any endogenous cell type?
What doses, routes and schedules were used, and what toxicity, cytokine and Treg/NK expansion readouts were seen in nonhuman primates?
How long did CAR-T expansion, B cell aplasia and tumor control last after dosing stopped, and did anti-drug antibodies develop?
cards.commercial_note: If the claim that CAR-T expansion and B cell aplasia occur without lymphodepletion holds in humans, it would remove chemotherapy conditioning from the treatment pathway, which is a meaningful differentiator, but the abstract gives no dose, safety or durability data to support that yet.

cards.title: Biodegradable lipid nanoparticles for genome editing in the brain via intrathecal administration.
cards.summary: The authors screened a 200-member library of biodegradable Passerini-derived ionizable lipids in vivo and identified P3B-LNPs that, given intrathecally, deliver Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA and adenine base editor mRNA to mouse brain, reaching 14.8% on-target correction in LumA reporter mice with better editing and tolerability than MC3.
cards.modality: LNP-delivered mRNA genome editing (Cas9 and adenine base editing)

facts.value: Biodegradable ionizable lipid nanoparticle, lead lipid P3B from a 200-member library
facts.quote: we synthesized a 200-member combinatorial library of structurally diverse, biodegradable ionizable lipids using the Passerini three-component reaction. High-throughput in vivo screening identified P3B

facts.value: Cas9 mRNA plus sgRNA; also adenine base editor mRNA
facts.quote: P3B-LNPs encapsulating Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA induced robust and widespread tdTomato expression

facts.value: Neurological diseases / CNS genome editing
facts.quote: therapeutic genome editing in neurological diseases

facts.value: Brain; neurons and astrocytes across multiple regions
facts.quote: tdTomato expression in neurons and astrocytes across multiple brain regions

facts.value: Ai9 reporter mice and LumA reporter mice
facts.quote: In Ai9 reporter mice, P3B-LNPs encapsulating Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA

facts.value: Intrathecal
facts.quote: Intrathecal administration provides a clinically validated route to bypass this barrier

facts.quote: restoring luciferase expression throughout the brain with 14.8% on-target correction and minimal off-target activity

facts.quote: enhanced tolerability, with attenuated inflammatory responses and a safety profile supportive of repeated dosing

facts.value: DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3)
facts.quote: substantially higher editing efficiency than the clinical benchmark DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3)

red_flags.why: mRNA dose per intrathecal injection is central to judging potency and translatability, and the abstract gives none.
The abstract reports no time points or persistence of editing or expression after dosing.

red_flags.quote: 14.8% on-target correction

red_flags.why: Group sizes for the in vivo screens and efficacy studies are not given.
Tolerability and repeat dosing support are asserted without specific markers, histology, or dosing schedule.
red_flags.quote: a safety profile supportive of repeated dosing

red_flags.why: Intrathecal volumes and CSF distribution differ greatly between mice and primates, so mouse data may not predict human dosing.
No encapsulation efficiency, particle size, or scale-up or yield data are reported.
"Minimal off-target activity" is stated without naming the method or genome-wide scope.
red_flags.quote: minimal off-target activity

open_questions: What mRNA dose and injection volume were used intrathecally, and how does editing scale with dose?
How long does editing and luciferase restoration persist, and what does a second dose add?
What fraction of neurons versus astrocytes in each brain region was edited, and how was off-target editing measured?
cards.commercial_note: A biodegradable LNP that beats MC3 for intrathecal CNS mRNA editing and tolerates repeat dosing could open redosable nonviral CNS editing, but the data so far are mouse reporter studies with 14.8% correction and no dose, durability, or large animal evidence.

cards.title: Tissue-specific silencing of synthetic mRNAs by de-targeting elements maps vaccination-competent tissues and allows Cas9 de-immunization.
cards.summary: The authors added tissue-specific microRNA target sites to the 3' UTR of LNP-delivered mRNAs to switch off expression in selected organs, found muscle and spleen are the tissues needed for priming immunity to a spike antigen, and applied the same de-targeting to Cas9 mRNA to lower its immunogenicity and toxicity.
cards.modality: mRNA/LNP delivery with miRNA-based tissue de-targeting, applied to vaccines and Cas9 genome editing

facts.value: mRNA in lipid nanoparticles, described as a gold-standard formulation
facts.quote: Using a gold-standard LNP formulation, we map exogenous mRNA biodistribution

facts.value: mRNAs with 3' UTR de-targeting elements that are target sites for endogenous tissue-specific microRNAs; payloads were a spike antigen and Cas9
facts.quote: we engineered mRNAs containing 3' UTR-embedded de-targeting elements as target sites for endogenous tissue-specific microRNAs, enabling selective silencing of antigen expression in defined anatomical compartments

facts.value: Vaccination (spike-based vaccine model) and in vivo genome editing
facts.quote: Applying this strategy to a spike-based vaccine model

facts.value: Muscle and spleen identified as the immunologically competent tissues for priming
facts.quote: we identify muscle and spleen as the most immunologically competent tissues required for robust immune priming

facts.value: De-targeting Cas9 mRNA from immune-active tissues reduced immunogenicity and toxicity
facts.quote: preventing mRNA-Cas9 expression in immune-active tissues, thereby reducing its immunogenicity and toxicity

facts.value: Claimed reduced immunogenicity and toxicity for Cas9, and reduced off-target effects as a design goal
facts.quote: enabling dose sparing and reduced off-target effects

red_flags.flag: No species or animal model stated
red_flags.why: Biodistribution and immune priming claims depend on the model used; the abstract does not say whether mice or another species were used.
mRNA/LNP dose and route drive both biodistribution and immunogenicity, and none are given.
Immune output comparisons across de-targeted organs need group sizes to be interpretable; none are reported.

red_flags.flag: Dose sparing is asserted, not demonstrated
red_flags.why: The abstract frames dose sparing as an enabled future benefit rather than a measured result.
red_flags.quote: enabling dose sparing and reduced off-target effects

red_flags.flag: Cas9 de-immunization claim lacks quantitative support
red_flags.why: No antibody titers, cytokine levels, liver enzyme values or editing efficiency are given to back the reduced immunogenicity and toxicity claim.
red_flags.quote: thereby reducing its immunogenicity and toxicity

red_flags.why: No follow-up time is given for antibody responses, editing, or silencing persistence.
Adding miRNA sites changes the mRNA construct; no data on translation loss in on-target tissues, purity or yield is reported.

red_flags.flag: miRNA de-targeting may trade potency for specificity
red_flags.why: Silencing antigen expression in some tissues could lower overall expression and efficacy, which the abstract does not quantify.

open_questions: What species, dose, route and group sizes were used for the biodistribution and immune priming experiments?
For de-targeted Cas9, what was the on-target editing efficiency in the intended tissue, and by how much did antibody titers, cytokines and toxicity markers fall?
Does miRNA de-targeting reduce total antigen expression or antibody titers compared to the unmodified mRNA, and over what follow-up period?
cards.commercial_note: If miRNA de-targeting elements can be dropped into existing mRNA/LNP constructs to cut Cas9 immunogenicity and toxicity without losing editing, it would be a low-cost, broadly licensable add-on to in vivo editing and vaccine programs, but the abstract gives no quantitative efficacy or safety numbers to size that benefit.

cards.title: Disruption of the CRL5 ubiquitin ligase complex enhances engineered T-cell persistence under chronic tumor antigen exposure.
cards.summary: Reanalysis of a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in primary human T cells identified the CRL5 complex, and knockout of its scaffold CUL5 improved serial tumor killing, reduced exhaustion markers across several CAR and TCR designs, and enriched BCMA CAR T cells in bone marrow with retained cytotoxicity after nearly 90 days in tumor-bearing mice.

facts.quote: In vivo, CUL5 knockout BCMA CAR T cells were enriched in the bone marrow following repeated tumor rechallenge

facts.value: sustained cytotoxicity, higher effector cytokines, fewer exhaustion marker-positive cells
facts.quote: CUL5 knockout T cells exhibited sustained cytotoxicity, elevated effector cytokine production, and fewer exhaustion marker-positive cells

cards.title: Long-term reversal of Duchenne muscular dystrophy via circular arRNA-guided exon skipping in monkeys and humans.
cards.summary: The authors used AAV-delivered circular ADAR-recruiting RNAs (LEAPER 2.0) to induce DMD exon skipping, reporting restored dystrophin and motor gains for at least 1.5 years in DMD nonhuman primates and dose-dependent exon skipping with functional gains in three patients after a single dose.

What AAV serotype, route and vector genome dose per kilogram were used, and what were liver enzyme, complement and anti-capsid findings?
What transcriptome-wide off-target RNA editing was seen, and how long were the three patients followed?
cards.commercial_note: A single-dose AAV product that restores dystrophin in hotspot mutations with 1.5 year durability in primates and early human functional gains would compete directly with weekly antisense oligonucleotides and with micro-dystrophin gene therapy, but with three patients and no disclosed dystrophin levels the data are far too early to value.

cards.title: Accelerated discovery of thermostable mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccines using data-efficient AI.

cards.commercial_note: Removing ultra-cold chain requirements for the two dominant clinical LNP compositions would matter for global vaccine distribution and for patch delivery, but the abstract gives no dose, antigen, safety or scale-up data to judge how close this is to a product.

cards.summary: In an open-label phase I/IIa trial, nine patients with biallelic PDE6A retinitis pigmentosa received a single subretinal injection of AAV8.hPDE6A at one of two doses, and over 1 year visual function did not improve while persistent adverse events included central retinal thinning and visual acuity loss.

cards.title: The Allogeneic FAP-CAR-IL15 iNKT Therapy MiNK-215 Remodels the Tumor Stroma to Enhance Antitumor Immunity.
cards.summary: The authors engineered allogeneic human iNKT cells to express a FAP-targeting CAR and secrete IL15 (MiNK-215), and report depletion of FAP+ CAFs, increased T-cell infiltration and antitumor activity in a mouse lung tumor model plus human organoid models of MSS colorectal cancer liver metastases.

cards.commercial_note: A named clinical candidate (MiNK-215) aimed at stroma-driven resistance in MSS colorectal cancer liver metastases addresses a segment with no effective immunotherapy, but the abstract offers only preclinical mouse and organoid data with no dose, persistence or manufacturing detail.

cards.title: Messenger RNA and guide RNA distributions in lipid nanoparticles impact gene-editing efficiency in vivo.
cards.summary: Using single-particle confocal spectroscopy, the authors measured how mRNA and guide RNA are distributed across individual LNPs made by three mixing methods and found that ALC-0315 LNPs with higher copies per co-encapsulated particle gave about 1.5-fold higher editing in mice (55.4% vs 36.3% indels) despite matched size and encapsulation.

Does the relationship between copies per particle and editing hold for DLin-MC3-DMA and at clinically relevant doses, and does higher loading affect tolerability?
cards.commercial_note: If per-particle payload distribution reliably predicts potency, CICS could become a release and process-development assay for LNP-CRISPR manufacturers, since the two batches here were indistinguishable by standard size and encapsulation measures yet differed 1.5-fold in editing.

red_flags.why: Base editor work reports on-target correction only, with no mention of genome-wide or bystander off-target analysis.

cards.title: Circular RNA vaccines encoding Pvs25 induce antibodies that block Plasmodium vivax transmission.
cards.summary: The authors made two circular RNA-LNP vaccines encoding Pvs25 (wild-type and MITD-fused) and showed in mice that a prime-boost regimen raised Pvs25 antibodies and completely blocked P. vivax development in mosquitoes, comparable to a linear mRNA-LNP comparator.

red_flags.why: RNA amount per immunization, route and boost interval are not stated, so potency cannot be judged.

red_flags.quote: elicited potent and durable transmission-blocking immunity in mice

open_questions: What RNA dose, route and prime-boost interval were used, and how many mice per group?
How long do antibody titers and transmission-blocking activity persist after the boost compared with linear mRNA?
What were circularization efficiency, purity and innate immune activation profiles of the circRNA batches?
cards.commercial_note: A transmission-blocking vaccine for P. vivax would enter a field with no approved product, and a circRNA platform could lower cost of goods, but the evidence here is mouse-only with no dose, durability or manufacturing data.

What safety, reactogenicity and biodistribution or persistence data were collected for LNP-dbDNA?
Does the durable response translate into protection in a challenge model, and how do HAI or neutralizing titers compare quantitatively?
cards.commercial_note: If dbDNA truly gives longer-lasting and more functional responses than mRNA at the same 20 ug dose in primates, it could compete as a nucleic acid vaccine backbone, but with no protection, safety or manufacturing data in the abstract the case rests on immunogenicity alone.

Do chip readouts rank-order vaccines or LNP formulations the same way as existing NHP or human clinical data?

cards.commercial_note: If the chip's rankings track in vivo outcomes, it could sell as a preclinical screening service to mRNA vaccine developers looking to cut NHP studies, but the abstract gives no validation against animal or clinical data to support that claim.

cards.title: Lipid nanoparticle-formulated synthetic messenger RNA induces reversible hematopoietic bias via type I interferon responses under upper-bound inflammatory conditions in preclinical animal models.
cards.summary: Intramuscular LNP-formulated mRNA at deliberately supra-clinical doses caused reversible suppression of erythroid lineage with granulocytic expansion in mouse and non-human primate bone marrow, an effect dependent on type I interferon signaling and resolving within 2 weeks.

cards.commercial_note: If high-dose systemic mRNA/LNP reliably triggers interferon-driven marrow lineage bias, developers of repeat-dose or high-dose nucleic acid therapeutics may face added preclinical hematology requirements, though the reported reversibility within 2 weeks and supra-clinical dosing limit the immediate regulatory impact.

cards.title: Genetic engineering of Staphylococcus haemolyticus: overcoming restriction-modification barriers and targeting virulence genes.
cards.summary: The authors mapped genomes and methylomes of nine clinical Staphylococcus haemolyticus isolates, then used SyngenicDNA motif removal plus a methylation-mimicking E. coli donor strain to bypass restriction-modification barriers and achieve the first targeted gene knockouts and allelic exchange in this species.
cards.modality: Bacterial genome engineering toolbox (not a human therapeutic)

red_flags.quote: lays a foundation for future functional studies of virulence and host adaptation

red_flags.why: Virulence genes were knocked out but the abstract does not state any animal or host-cell infection experiment showing a phenotype.

red_flags.quote: These tools significantly enhanced transformation efficiency

red_flags.why: Nine isolates were sequenced but the abstract does not state in how many strains editing actually worked.

red_flags.quote: a Type II (PDLC03279) and a Type III (PDL3649/PDLC03643) system were significantly overrepresented in clinical isolates

cards.title: Multiplexed lipid nanoparticle barcoding reveals tissue-dynamic kinetic insights and enriched cellular tropism in hepatic zones.
cards.summary: The authors built a barcoded Cre recombinase mRNA screening platform that lets many LNP formulations be tracked at once in tdTomato reporter mice, and used it to measure mRNA accumulation and degradation kinetics in liver, lung and spleen and to find formulations with hepatic zonal bias and unnoticed extrahepatic tropism.

Number of animals per group and number of formulations screened are not given.

Degradation kinetics are mentioned but no time points or duration of expression are given.

cards.title: A modular γδ TCR-T platform combining KRAS pMHC targeting with re-dosable mRNA engager redirection.

facts.quote: We knocked the KRASG12V/HLA-A*11:01 TCR A11v into primary human γδ T cells.

A secreted CD3 engager produced systemically raises cytokine release and on-target off-tumor mesothelin toxicity risk, and none is reported.

open_questions: What cell dose, LNP dose and redosing interval were used, and how long does circulating engager persist after each dose?
